Learning Bayesian modelling with NBA vs EuroLeague data

A guided tour of every model in this project

Code 
source(here::here("R", "config.R"))
source(here::here("R", "metrics.R"))
source(here::here("R", "bayes.R"))
source(here::here("R", "data.R"))
source(here::here("R", "theme.R"))
suppressMessages({ library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(bayesplot) })
theme_set(theme_project())
tg <- load_team_games(SEASONS_LONG)

This notebook is a companion to the analysis scripts. Every section takes one model used in the project, explains it in words, and shows how to check that it does what we think it does. The order goes from simple to more advanced:

# Model Where it is used New idea
1 Season means around a line RQ2, replication of the 2019 paper Hierarchical model, sufficient statistics, centred vs non-centred
2 Mixed model with team/opponent effects RQ1, RQ3 Random effects, priors on a standardised scale, posterior contrasts
3 Binomial model with logit link RQ1/RQ3 shot zones Generalised linear models, overdispersion
4 Random-walk smooth trend RQ2 Latent time series, controlling wiggliness with a prior
5 Shift model with a discrete lag RQ2 Marginalising out a discrete parameter
6 2-D spatial smooth RQ1 accuracy surface Splines in brms

The workflow is the same for all of them: write the model → choose priors → check priors make sense → fit → check the sampler (R-hat, ESS, divergences) → check the fit to data (posterior predictive) → read the posterior.

1. The 2019 paper’s model: season means around a line

The model

For one league and one variable (say possessions per game), game \(i\) in season \(j\):

\[ y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_j, \sigma_j), \qquad \mu_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu + s\,(t_j - 2008),\ \sigma) \]

Two levels: games scatter around their season mean \(\mu_j\); season means scatter around a straight line with intercept \(\mu\) and slope \(s\). This is a hierarchical model: the season means are parameters, and they share information through the line.

Trick 1: sufficient statistics

The NBA has ~2,500 team-games per season. Fitting the game-level model directly (brms: bf(y ~ 1 + t_c + (1 | season), sigma ~ 0 + season)) took over 10 minutes per fit. But if games within a season are i.i.d. normal, the count, mean and variance of each season contain all the information about \(\mu_j\) and \(\sigma_j\):

\[ \bar y_j \sim \text{Normal}\!\left(\mu_j, \tfrac{\sigma_j}{\sqrt{n_j}}\right), \qquad \frac{(n_j-1)\,s_j^2}{\sigma_j^2} \sim \chi^2_{n_j-1} \]

So RQ2_trends_leadlag/models/paper_trend.stan takes 3 numbers per season instead of 2,500 and returns the same posterior in about a second. Read the Stan file: note the extra log(n - 1) - 2 * log(sigma_j) term. That is the Jacobian, needed because we put a density on \(s_j^2\) but wrote it as a \(\chi^2\) density of a transformed quantity.

Did it work? Replicating Table 1

Code 
rep <- read.csv(here::here("RQ2_trends_leadlag/results/tables/replication_vs_published.csv"))
summarise(rep, max_abs_diff = max(abs(mean - published)), max_rhat = max(max_rhat))
  max_abs_diff max_rhat
1    0.0128553 1.010669

All 68 estimates match the paper to within rounding. Always validate a model on data where you know the answer before using it on new data.

Lesson: centred vs non-centred parameterisation

A few fits first showed divergent transitions: the sampler hits a region of very high curvature. This happens when the between-season SD \(\sigma\) approaches 0 (the “funnel”). The textbook fix is the non-centred form, \(\mu_j = \mu + s\,t_j + \sigma z_j\) with \(z_j \sim N(0,1)\). We tried it, and it was worse (R-hat up to 1.22). Why? Non-centring helps when the data say little about each \(\mu_j\). Here every season mean is pinned down by thousands of games, so the centred form is better. We kept the centred form and raised adapt_delta to 0.99 (smaller, more careful steps); 16 divergences remained out of 340,000 draws. The right parameterisation depends on how informative the data are.

2. Mixed models with team and opponent effects (RQ1, RQ3)

The model

bf(z ~ 0 + league + (1 | team_season) + (1 | opp_season), sigma ~ 0 + league)
  • z is the metric standardised (mean 0, SD 1). Then a prior like normal(0, 1.5) on the league means is sensible for every metric: free throws per foul or minutes entropy alike.
  • (1 | team_season): each team-season has its own level, drawn from a normal distribution whose SD is estimated. Games of one team are correlated; ignoring that would make us overconfident.
  • (1 | opp_season): the opponent matters too (blocks depend on who you play).
  • sigma ~ 0 + league: the game-to-game noise may differ by league (distributional regression).

Prior predictive check

Before fitting, simulate data from the priors alone and ask: is this plausible?

Code 
d <- tg |> filter(season %in% TODAY_SEASONS, phase == "regular") |>
  mutate(z = (pace40 - mean(pace40, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(pace40, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  filter(is.finite(z)) |> slice_sample(n = 2000)
pp <- brm(bf(z ~ 0 + league + (1 | team_season) + (1 | opp_season), sigma ~ 0 + league),
          data = d, sample_prior = "only", chains = 1, iter = 600, refresh = 0, seed = 1, silent = 2,
          prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"), prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sd"),
                    prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "sigma")))
pp_check(pp, ndraws = 30) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-15, 15)) +
  labs(title = "Prior predictive: simulated z-scores vs the real data (dark line)")

The priors allow a wide range of values, including some silly ones (|z| of 10), but they don’t rule out anything realistic. That is what weakly informative means.

Checking a fitted model

Code 
fit <- readRDS(file.path(DATA_ROOT, "RQ1", "models", "box_pace40.rds"))
diagnostics(fit)
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  max_rhat min_ess_bulk min_ess_tail divergences
     <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>
1     1.01         390.         808.           0
Code 
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 30) + labs(title = "Posterior predictive check: pace per 40 min")
  • R-hat ≈ 1.00: the 4 chains agree. Values above 1.01 mean “run longer or fix the model”.
  • ESS (effective sample size): the number of independent draws the chains are worth. Bulk-ESS above ~400 is enough for means and intervals.
  • Divergences: should be 0.
  • pp_check: data simulated from the fitted model should look like the real data.

Reading the posterior: contrasts

The question “how much faster is the NBA?” is a function of parameters, so we compute it draw by draw and summarise at the end:

Code 
dr <- as_draws_df(fit)
today <- tg |> filter(season %in% TODAY_SEASONS, phase == "regular", is.finite(pace40))
s <- sd(today$pace40)   # the SD used to standardise; differences only need the scale
diff <- s * (dr$b_leagueNBA - dr$b_leagueEuroLeague)
c(mean = mean(diff), quantile(diff, c(.025, .975)), P_NBA_faster = mean(diff > 0))
        mean         2.5%        97.5% P_NBA_faster 
   10.356951     9.283435    11.395590     1.000000

There’s no p-value and no t-test: the posterior of the difference is the answer, including statements like “probability the NBA is faster”.

3. Binomial models: shot zones

Counts out of totals (corner threes out of all shots; makes out of attempts) are binomial:

bf(n_zone | trials(n_total) ~ 0 + league + (1 | team_season)), family = binomial()

The coefficients live on the logit scale; plogis() turns them into probabilities. The team-season random effect is important: without it the model treats 200,000 NBA shots as independent, and the intervals become absurdly narrow. Real teams differ in style, so the effective sample size is closer to the number of teams than of shots.

Code 
read.csv(here::here("RQ1_differences_today/results/tables/shot_zones_today.csv")) |>

4. Smooth trends: a second-order random walk

The 2019 model forces a straight line. The NBA’s three-point growth is not straight. The RW2 model (season_curve.stan) says the trend keeps its slope unless the data push it:

\[ f_t = 2 f_{t-1} - f_{t-2} + \omega\,\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim N(0,1) \]

\(\omega\) controls wiggliness: \(\omega=0\) gives a straight line (the 2019 model is a special case), large \(\omega\) follows every bump. We put a half-normal(0, 0.3) prior on \(\omega\) (on the standardised scale), which prefers smooth curves, and let the data decide.

Code 
sm <- season_means(tg |> filter(league == "NBA", phase == "regular", season %in% SEASONS), "p3a_share")
f <- fit_season_curve(sm)
tibble(season = sm$season, obs = sm$mean, fit = colMeans(f),
       lo = apply(f, 2, quantile, .025), hi = apply(f, 2, quantile, .975)) |>
  ggplot(aes(season)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = .2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit)) + geom_point(aes(y = obs)) +
  labs(title = "NBA: share of shots from three, RW2 trend", y = NULL)

A lesson learned the hard way. The first version sampled the curve \(f\) directly. When \(\omega\) is small, all the \(f_t\) are tied together. That is the funnel again, and it gave divergences and R-hat up to 1.3 in both the centred and the non-centred form. The fix: everything in this model is Gaussian, so \(f\) can be integrated out with pen and paper. Writing \(f = M u\) with \(u = (f_1, \text{slope}, \varepsilon_3, \dots)\), the season means are jointly \(\text{MultiNormal}(0,\ M D M^\top + R)\), where \(D = \text{diag}(4, 1, \omega^2, \dots)\) and \(R = \text{diag}(se^2 + \tau^2)\). Stan then only samples \(\omega\) and \(\tau\) (no funnel left), and draws of \(f\) are generated afterwards from the exact Gaussian conditional \(f \mid y\). Result: 0 divergences and R-hat ≤ 1.005. When part of a model is Gaussian, integrating it out is often the best reparameterisation of all. The lead–lag model (next section) uses the same trick.

A neat consequence: because we have draws of the whole curve, any question about it has a posterior. “Did the gap between leagues shrink?” is just mean(abs(gap_2025) < abs(gap_2010)) over the draws.

5. A discrete parameter: the lag between leagues

The shift model (lead_lag.stan) asks whether the EuroLeague’s curve is the NBA’s curve shifted by \(k\) seasons. \(k\) is an integer, and Stan’s sampler (HMC) needs continuous parameters. The solution is to marginalise: sum the likelihood over all values of \(k\),

\[ p(\text{data}) = \sum_{k=-5}^{5} p(k)\, p(\text{data} \mid k), \]

which in Stan is target += log_sum_exp(lp). In generated quantities we recover \(P(k \mid \text{data})\) with softmax(lp). This is the same trick used for mixture models and change-point models.

Caution. With ~25 seasons, a smooth trend can often be shifted a few years either way and still fit. A flat posterior over \(k\) is an honest “the data can’t tell”, not a failure.

6. A 2-D smooth: accuracy across the court

bf(made | trials(n) ~ league + t2(x_abs, y, by = league, k = 8)), family = binomial()

t2() is a tensor-product spline: a flexible surface over the court. brms turns the spline wiggliness into a random effect (the sds parameters), so the amount of smoothing is estimated, not chosen by hand. We count shots on a 0.5 m grid first: the binomial likelihood of a cell with 300 shots is exactly the product of 300 Bernoulli likelihoods, but 1,000× faster. This is the same idea as the sufficient statistics in Section 1.

7. Shrinkage without MCMC: conjugate priors (RQ4)

RQ4 needs a style profile for about 8,600 player-seasons and team-seasons. A player with 60 shots who took 40% of them from the corner is probably not a corner specialist; he is probably just lucky. Shrinkage pulls small samples towards the average, and pulls large samples hardly at all.

Some prior-likelihood pairs give a posterior in the same family as the prior: they are conjugate, and the posterior can be written down directly, with no sampling algorithm:

data prior posterior
zone counts \(n_1..n_5\) ~ Multinomial(\(p\)) \(p\) ~ Dirichlet(\(\alpha m\)) Dirichlet(\(\alpha m + n\))
assists \(y\) ~ Poisson(\(\lambda E\)), \(E\) = possessions \(\lambda\) ~ Gamma(\(\kappa\), \(\kappa/\mu\)) Gamma(\(\kappa + y\), \(\kappa/\mu + E\))

Read the Dirichlet posterior as “the prior is worth \(\alpha\) imaginary shots” taken with the league’s average shot mix \(m\). With \(\alpha = 100\), a player with 60 real shots would end up closer to the league average than to his own numbers; with 1,000 shots his own numbers would dominate. In practice the data choose small values (7–26 shots, below): players at the same position really do take very different shots, so the prior is weak and only small samples are pulled noticeably.

Who chooses \(\alpha\)? The data do. Across all players, the marginal likelihood of the counts (the Dirichlet-multinomial, i.e. the likelihood with \(p\) integrated out) depends only on \(\alpha\). Maximising it is empirical Bayes. It is the same “integrate out, then fit” idea as Section 4, and it is what a full hierarchical model would do, but with \(\alpha\) fixed at its best value rather than given its own prior.

Code 
read.csv(here::here("RQ4_ahead_of_their_time/results/tables/player_prior_strength.csv")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x)))
      league position dirichlet_alpha ast tov orb drb blk stl pf ftr
1        NBA        C               7   4  12   9  19   5   9 18   6
2        NBA        F               9   5   9   4  13   3  11 13   6
3        NBA        G              17   4   8   5  16   3  12 19   6
4 EuroLeague        C               7   6  13  13  30   3  13 14   7
5 EuroLeague        F              15   6  11   5  15   2  15 16   5
6 EuroLeague        G              26   5  10   5  17   1  10 17   6

dirichlet_alpha is the prior’s weight in shots, per league and position. The other columns are \(\kappa\) for each rate. Because posteriors are closed-form, R/style.R draws 300–400 samples per player in a fraction of a second. Each draw is pushed through the rest of the analysis (distances, time positions), so every RQ4 number has a credible interval. “P(most typical)” is simply the share of draws in which a player is the closest to the league average.

What we gave up. Empirical Bayes treats \(\alpha\) and \(\kappa\) as known, so intervals are a little too narrow. With hundreds of players per league that error is small; with ten it would not be.
